domains.title: Messenger of Frigg
domains.subtitle: Swift Errand-Runner Across Worlds
domains.lead: Gná is one of the Ásynjur, the goddesses of the Norse pantheon, and the special messenger of Frigg. Her horse, Hofvarpnir, runs through air and over sea, carrying her wherever the queen of the gods sends her. She is not a warrior or a mother in the surviving sources; she is speed, service, and the unseen thread that keeps the divine household in motion.

cards.name: Hofvarpnir
cards.desc: Her horse, born of Hófvarpni and Hamskerpir, can gallop through the sky and across the waves.

cards.name: Errands of Frigg
cards.desc: Gná carries the queen's word to every corner of the cosmos, the diplomatic courier of Ásgarðr.

cards.name: The Falling Gná
cards.desc: A farmer once mocked her from a fence; she made the fence-post fall, teaching him to respect a goddess.

cards.name: Swift as Wind
cards.desc: She is the answer Frigg gives when asked which Ásynjur can be trusted to move between worlds without delay.

mythology.lead: Gná's mythology is compact to the point of austerity: the entire narrative record is one chapter of Snorri's catalogue of the Ásynjur (Gylfaginning 35) and the name-lists of the þulur. Speed is her being, her horse Hofvarpnir her attribute, and one fallen fence her single miracle — a minor goddess with exactly enough story to be unforgettable.

myths.title: The Queen's Own Courier
myths.text: Snorri's catalogue gives Gná a single function and lets it define her: 'Gná is the name of one of them; Frigg sends her into various worlds on her errands. She has the horse Hofvarpnir, which runs through the air and over the sea' (Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35, Faulkes trans.). Wherever Frigg's word must travel — to the other halls of the gods, out among the giants, to whatever errand queens cannot ride to themselves — Gná is the one who carries it, and the carrying is her whole being. The myth is spare because the office is: a messenger is pure function, speed in the service of someone else's will. The Edda honours that function with a goddess of its own, and in doing so admits that the errands of the great are themselves divine work.

myths.title: Born of the Wind
myths.text: Snorri does not leave Hofvarpnir's pedigree to guesswork: the sky-runner 'is produced by Hófvarpni and Hamskerpir' (Gylfaginning 35; cf. the þulur lists of mythic horse-names) — two otherwise unknown horses whose mating produced a foal that runs on air and sea alike, unbothered by the boundary that stops ordinary hooves. The detail is Eddic in its economy: even a minor goddess's mount gets a genealogy, because in this world everything worth naming is born of something named. Hofvarpnir — the name suggests 'hoof-thrower' — is the divine household's answer to distance itself, and Gná's whole horizon is the ground such a horse can erase between one world and the next.

myths.title: The Falling Fence
myths.text: Snorri's one anecdote about Gná is her only recorded miracle. Riding past a farm, she heard a man call from his fence: who rides there? She answered that it was Gná, sent on Frigg's errands. The man mocked her — the fence stood too high for any horse to leap it. Gná reached out, and 'the fence-post fell, and the fence with it', and she rode on through the gap (Gylfaginning 35). The scene is comedy with a blade in it: the sceptic measures a goddess by an obstacle, and the obstacle is removed. The Edda's lesson is about rank and power — even the least of the Ásynjur holds dominion over the fixed world the moment she is mocked, and mockery of a goddess is itself a kind of falling fence.

myths.title: A Name in the Lists
myths.text: Beyond Gylfaginning 35, Gná survives only in the name-lists — the þulur catalogues of the goddesses appended to the Prose Edda manuscripts — and in later glosses of the word itself, whose exact sense is uncertain; Cleasby–Vigfusson connect it with the notion of projecting or gazing out. The record should be stated plainly: one passage, one anecdote, one horse. Everything else said about her is modern inference — which is precisely why poets and novelists have made her their own, writing into the silence what the skalds left out: the errands themselves, the worlds at the far end of them, and the speed of a goddess who exists, fully and only, on the way.

lore.syncretism: Gná has no clear foreign double, but her function — the divine messenger riding a supernatural horse — places her in a common Germanic and Indo-European type. The Vedic Pūṣan and Greek Hermês are wandering messengers with swift horses or sandals; the Irish Manannán rides Aonbharr over sea and land. Within Norse mythology, her closest counterpart is the god Hermóðr, who rides to Hel to bargain for Baldr. Gná is the feminine form of the type: not a psychopomp, but the queen's own courier.
lore.culturalLegacy: Gná remains a minor but beloved figure in modern retellings of Norse myth. Her name is sometimes given to characters who embody swiftness or loyal service, and her horse Hofvarpnir appears in games and fiction as a mount that can run on air. In Heathen practice she is occasionally invoked for matters of communication, travel, and the safe delivery of messages. Restoring Gná preserves the acute accent and long vowel that mark her as one of the Ásynjur rather than a modern abbreviation.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Gná is the goddess of the reliable message. She does not decide what is said; she makes sure it arrives. In a pantheon full of warriors and kings, she is the one who keeps the lines open — the diplomatic pouch, the swift horse, the word that cannot be delayed.

Her one recorded miracle is the falling fence: when a man doubted her passage, the obstacle removed itself. The story is a lesson in the power of divine errand-runners and in the folly of measuring a goddess by her apparent rank. Speed, attention, and faithful delivery are her virtues, and they are rarer than they look.

lore.archaeology: Gná is a purely textual figure. No runestone, image, or place-name is securely hers. Her only witnesses are the manuscripts of Snorri's Prose Edda and the associated þulur name-lists.
